extracted.intended_audience: speculative fiction writers (fantasy & science fiction) worldbuilding religions and rituals
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for creating believable, useful religions and rituals in fantasy and science fiction, covering why to include religion, how to design its epistemology and practices, and how to research and portray it respectfully. Emphasizes worldbuilding techniques, characterization, and ethical considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reflect real-world religiosity
rubrics_metrics.description: Most people are religious to some degree; speculative fiction can and often should reflect that aspect of humanity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use religion in your world because it mirrors how humans look for patterns and meaning. Including religion makes societies feel realistic and gives you material to explore beliefs and behaviors rather than avoiding religion because the genre historically skews areligious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use religion as a source of conflict and motivation
rubrics_metrics.description: Religion is a strong source of conflict and can explain actions and motivations of characters and groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leverage religious differences, rituals, and identity to create plot conflict and to show moral complexity: 'make sure that they are shades of gray, not white or black.' Use historical or invented sectarian tensions to reveal character choices and community dynamics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Start with epistemology (how people know/believe things)
rubrics_metrics.description: Build religions by asking: how do these people know things and why do they believe them? Treat religion as an epistemology—ways of knowing, accepting evidence, and trusting authorities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask what evidences the culture accepts, how belief is transmitted, and whether beliefs are falsifiable or based on authority/tradition. Beginning at the epistemological level leads to more interesting, internally consistent religions than simply mapping existing religions onto your world.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider how visible gods or magic change religious structure
rubrics_metrics.description: In settings where gods appear or magic is demonstrable, religion functions differently: the presence of visible divine power alters ritual, doctrine, and doubt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask questions like 'Are there atheists in a world where gods appear?' or 'How does visible divine action affect priestly authority or organized religion?' Use those answers to shape institutions, practices, and social reactions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't map directly onto a real religion unless you can do it respectfully and accurately
rubrics_metrics.description: Using an existing religion wholesale is acceptable only when the author understands it deeply and can portray it realistically and respectfully.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you choose to base a fictional religion on a real one, be aware of authorial perspective (e.g., Katherine Kurtz successfully adapted Catholicism because she could write it authentically). Avoid careless copying that misrepresents or offends; ensure nuance and respect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use random generators or improv to kickstart original elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Start with odd, bare-bones prompts (e.g., 'birthdays important, hate holidays, birds are virtue symbols') then connect them into a coherent system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Random combinations force unexpected connections and help create religions that don't mimic Earth ones. Treat it like an improv game: collect disparate traits and find plausible cultural logics that link them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build rituals and religious language organically from culture-specific facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Let physical anatomy, counting systems, language, and material culture inform religious symbols, names, and rituals so they feel authentic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: creating a numbering system for an alien species and deriving numerology/ritual language from that makes spiritual language feel real. Work from linguistic and cultural roots rather than inventing arbitrary-sounding terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research unusual real-world practices as jumping-off points
rubrics_metrics.description: Study obscure or surprising customs in actual religions to inspire fictional rituals, then alter them so their origin isn't directly identifiable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use real-world oddities (e.g., coming-of-age practices) for ideas, but change details to avoid direct appropriation and to remain respectful. The goal is inspiration, not copying.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show religion through action and cultural participation, not just doctrine
rubrics_metrics.description: Define religiousness by what people do daily—their rituals, communal behaviors, and cultural participation—rather than only by formal creeds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Depict rituals, church attendance patterns, community activities, and how religion structures everyday life. This approach yields authentic portrayals rooted in practice rather than abstract belief statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat non-falsifiable beliefs with respect; satirize only dishonesty or hypocrisy
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid mocking non-falsifiable elements of belief systems; the permitted target is inconsistency or deliberate self-deception used to manipulate others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be empathetic toward beliefs that lack empirical proof. If you critique religion in fiction, focus on hypocrisy or dishonesty ('lying to themselves to forward some sort of an agenda') rather than ridiculing faith itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be mindful of your own cultural/religious bias and limited experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Your personal experience of religion (attendance style, rituals, emphasis) may not generalize; don't assume your mode of participation is universal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize diversity within and between faiths; consult sources or attend different services to avoid projecting your experience onto all practitioners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use ritual details to reveal character and social structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Rituals, taboos, and ceremonial roles can be tools to show character beliefs, social roles, power dynamics, and cultural priorities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design rituals to have narratively useful consequences—what someone must do, suffer, or sacrifice reveals motivations and can drive plot. Small ritual details (numbers, objects, sequences) can encode social information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider political/theocratic uses and potential for oppression
rubrics_metrics.description: Religion can be institutionalized for control; theocratic governments and rituals can enforce social order and strip rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use examples like The Handmaid’s Tale to explore how ritual and law intertwine to oppress; think through how religious law affects gender, property, reproduction, and civic life in your world.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create cultural markers (numerology, holidays, taboos) for distinctiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Develop holidays, taboos, symbols, and numerological associations that set a religion apart and make it culturally legible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small systems (e.g., what numbers mean, which animals are virtuous) give texture. Ensure these markers arise logically from the culture's history, environment, or physiology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn by observing real religious practice (assigned homework)
rubrics_metrics.description: Experience a worship service or religious meeting different from your own to understand how people live their faith.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attend as an observer—note rituals, language, communal dynamics, and what feels similar/different from your expectations. Use that firsthand insight to inform empathetic, realistic portrayals.
